_comment: Species deliberately kept OUT of the native-plant catalogue, with the reason and the authority for each. src/data_quality.py:validate_excluded_taxa fails the build if one reappears in data/plants_master.json, data/garden_plants.json or as the `plant` of an edge in data/plant_fauna_master.json.
_why_this_file_exists: A plant is removed once and can come back many times. Rudbeckia hirta shipped flagged `native_to_alberta = 1` and noted 'Classic prairie wildflower', so nothing in the app disagreed with it — and data/fetched/fauna_edges_candidates.json still holds 389 GloBI records naming it, ready to be re-proposed by the next sourcing pass. A deletion with no record of the decision is an invitation to redo it.
_scope: This is NOT a nativity gate. It is a list of specific calls that were made, each with its evidence. A species absent from the catalogue and absent from here has simply never been considered.
_p9: `authority` names who says so. Where the authorities disagree the entry says so rather than picking one silently — see docs/DESIGN_PHILOSOPHY.md P9.

taxa.authority: VASCAN (Database of Vascular Plants of Canada) records Rudbeckia hirta as introduced in AB, SK, MB and BC, and native from Ontario eastward. Moss, Flora of Alberta, agrees: introduced. It is a garden and wildflower-mix escape here, not a member of any Alberta plant community.
taxa.disagreement: Occurrence data does not settle this and should not be read as if it did — the plant_ecoregions entry removed with this row carried 215 georeferenced GBIF records across eight prairie ecoregions, 102 of them in Aspen Parkland. That is what a widely-planted self-seeder looks like. Presence is not nativity; see src/establishment.py.
taxa.took_with_it: 150 documented plant-fauna edges, 1 plant_ecoregions entry, 2 seeded polyculture memberships and 1 worked-example fallback.
taxa.substitute: Ratibida columnifera (Prairie Coneflower) — the native yellow-rayed, dark-coned composite it was standing in for, at a similar height and bloom window.

taxa.authority: VASCAN (Database of Vascular Plants of Canada) records Helianthus giganteus from eastern Canada — Ontario eastward through Quebec and the Maritimes — and not from Alberta or Saskatchewan. Moss, Flora of Alberta, does not treat it. The prairies' tall native sunflowers are H. nuttallii and H. maximiliani, both already in the catalogue; the seed row's own note ('Tall perennial sunflower... major late-season pollinator and bird food') describes those equally well, which is how the wrong binomial went unquestioned.
taxa.disagreement: The internal evidence is CONSISTENT with this but does not settle it, and the difference from Rudbeckia hirta is worth keeping. That removal was made against 215 georeferenced records: occurrence disagreed and lost, because presence is not nativity. Here there is no entry in data/plant_ecoregions.json at all — and the derived file records only species WITH rows, so an absence there means either no records inside the polygons or a fetch GBIF refused, and the file cannot tell them apart after the fact (see seed_ecoregion_ranges.FetchFailed). So the call rests on the authority, with the internal silence noted as agreeing rather than as proving.
taxa.not_machine_verified: This container's egress policy answers 403 to CONNECT for data.canadensys.net, so VASCAN was cited here and not queried. From a machine with open egress, https://data.canadensys.net/vascan/api/0.1/search.json?q=Helianthus+giganteus returns the record in one request — and scripts/fetch_flora_nativity.py (F137) asks it for the whole catalogue at once, which is the point.
taxa.took_with_it: 11 documented plant-fauna edges (10 nectar, 1 seed_food; 8 from iNaturalist via GloBI, 2 Bumble Bee Watch, 1 Cornell Birds of the World) and 1 seeded polyculture membership. No animal was left without an edge, unlike V2.74, which orphaned six.
taxa.substitute: Nuttall's Sunflower (Helianthus nuttallii) — the native tall sunflower of prairie wet meadows and sloughs, same August-September bloom, same bird_food / keystone_species / pollinator uses.
